Problem Statement¶

Context

AlphaCom is a leading telecommunications provider experiencing an increase in customer churn, which is affecting its revenue and brand reputation. Customer churn can be influenced by several factors, including service usage, billing preferences, contract types, and customer demographics. The existing customer-retention approach is primarily reactive, with action being taken after customers have already decided to leave. This makes it difficult for AlphaCom to identify customers who are at risk of churning in advance. Therefore, the project focuses on developing a Customer Churn Prediction model that can identify customers who are likely to churn and help understand the key factors associated with their churn.

Objective of the Study

The primary objective of this project is to develop a predictive model that can identify customers who are at high risk of churn and understand the key factors influencing customer churn. The analysis aims to help AlphaCom: • Identify customers who are likely to churn. • Understand the key factors associated with customer churn. • Support proactive and targeted customer-retention strategies. • Reduce potential churn-related revenue losses. • Improve customer lifetime value.

Need of the Study / Project

Customer churn can have a direct impact on the revenue and long-term growth of a telecommunications company. If customers who are likely to leave can be identified in advance, the company can take appropriate retention actions before the customer churns. This study is therefore needed to analyze customer characteristics and service-related factors associated with churn and develop a predictive approach that can help AlphaCom prioritize customers who require retention efforts.

Business Opportunity

The project provides AlphaCom with an opportunity to adopt a proactive, data-driven approach to customer retention. By identifying customers who are at a higher risk of churn, the company can focus its retention efforts on the customers who need attention and take appropriate actions before they leave. This can potentially help AlphaCom improve customer retention, protect revenue, and improve customer lifetime value.

• There are 127 records with negative tenure values. Out of these, 103 records have a tenure of -1, 23 records have -2, and 1 record has -3.

• Since tenure represents the number of months a customer has been with the company, these values are not valid and need to be handled.

In [23]:
# Calculate median tenure using only valid tenure values
valid_tenure = df1['tenure'].where(df1['tenure'] >= 0)

tenure_median = valid_tenure.groupby(df1['Contract']).transform('median')

# Identify negative tenure values
negative_tenure = df1['tenure'] < 0

# Replace negative tenure with the Contract-wise median
df1.loc[negative_tenure, 'tenure'] = tenure_median[negative_tenure]
In [24]:
print("Minimum tenure:", df1['tenure'].min())
print("Negative tenure values:", (df1['tenure'] < 0).sum())

Minimum tenure: 0.0
Negative tenure values: 0

Treatment of Negative Tenure Values:

• The tenure variable contained 127 negative values, which are logically invalid because tenure represents the number of months a customer has been associated with the company. The invalid values were identified and directly replaced with the median tenure of the corresponding contract group. The median was calculated using only valid, non-negative tenure values.

• Contract-wise median imputation was used because customer tenure may vary across different contract types. This approach preserves the variation in tenure across customer contract groups while avoiding the use of a single overall median

• After treatment, the minimum tenure was 0 months and no negative tenure values remained.

• Logical consistency checks were performed between related service variables to identify potential data-quality anomalies. The analysis compared PhoneService with MultipleLines and InternetService with OnlineSecurity, OnlineBackup, DeviceProtection, TechSupport, StreamingTV, and StreamingMovies.

• The results identified some unusual combinations, such as customers with PhoneService = No but MultipleLines = Yes, customers with PhoneService = Yes but MultipleLines = No phone service, and customers with InternetService = No but certain additional services marked as Yes or No.

• These combinations were flagged for further investigation, as they may represent data inconsistencies or may have a valid business explanation, such as access through an alternative internet connection.

In [41]:
# Identify potentially inconsistent Internet Service records

internet_anomalies = pd.DataFrame()

for col in internet_service_checks:
    # InternetService = No should normally have "No internet service"
    condition_no_internet = (
        (df1['InternetService'] == 'No') &
        (df1[col] != 'No internet service')
    )

    # InternetService = DSL/Fiber optic should normally not have "No internet service"
    condition_with_internet = (
        (df1['InternetService'].isin(['DSL', 'Fiber optic'])) &
        (df1[col] == 'No internet service')
    )

    temp = df1[condition_no_internet | condition_with_internet].copy()
    temp['Inconsistent_Variable'] = col

    internet_anomalies = pd.concat(
        [internet_anomalies, temp],
        axis=0
    )

print("Total potentially inconsistent records:", len(internet_anomalies))

print("\nInconsistencies by variable:")
print(internet_anomalies['Inconsistent_Variable'].value_counts())

# Treat InternetService-related inconsistencies

for col in internet_service_checks:

    # Customers without InternetService

    df1.loc[
        df1['InternetService'] == 'No',
        col
    ] = 'No internet service'

    # Customers with DSL/Fiber optic have internet service,
    # so "No internet service" is changed to "No"
    df1.loc[
        (df1['InternetService'].isin(['DSL', 'Fiber optic'])) &
        (df1[col] == 'No internet service'),
        col
    ] = 'No'

Currency Standardisation of Charge Variables

In [63]:
# Currency conversion rates to USD
# Rates checked on 16 September 2026 using XE
EUR_TO_USD = 1.1542
GBP_TO_USD = 1.3478

def convert_to_usd(value):
    if pd.isna(value):
        return np.nan

    value = str(value).strip()

    # Preserve missing-like values as missing
    if value.lower() in ['nan', 'none', '']:
        return np.nan

    # Convert GBP to USD
    if value.startswith('£'):
        number = value.replace('£', '').strip()
        return float(number) * GBP_TO_USD

    # Convert EUR to USD
    elif value.startswith('€'):
        number = value.replace('€', '').strip()
        return float(number) * EUR_TO_USD

    # USD values: remove $ only
    elif value.startswith('$'):
        number = value.replace('$', '').strip()
        return float(number)

    # Already numeric
    else:
        return pd.to_numeric(value, errors='coerce')


# Apply currency conversion
for col in ['MonthlyCharges', 'TotalCharges']:
    df1[col] = df1[col].apply(convert_to_usd)


# Check data types
print("Data types after currency standardisation:")
print(df1[['MonthlyCharges', 'TotalCharges']].dtypes)

# Check missing values
print("\nMissing values:")
print(df1[['MonthlyCharges', 'TotalCharges']].isna().sum())

Currency Standardisation and Data Type Correction:

• The monetary variables, MonthlyCharges and TotalCharges, were standardised to a single currency (USD) to ensure consistency because the dataset contains multiple currency formats.

• Currency symbols were removed only after applying the appropriate currency conversion, and both variables were converted to a numerical float64 data type for further statistical analysis. Existing missing values were retained for subsequent missing-value treatment.

# Calculate median using valid (non-negative) TotalCharges
valid_total_charges = df1.loc[
    (~negative_total) & (df1['TotalCharges'].notna()),
    'TotalCharges'
]

# Impute negative TotalCharges with the median

• A total of 147 negative TotalCharges records were identified and assessed using contract type, churn status, and tenure. As the available variables did not provide sufficient evidence to establish a valid business explanation for these negative cumulative charges, the anomalous values were treated using median imputation.

• The median of the valid TotalCharges observations was 1,373.0, which was used to replace the negative values. After treatment, no negative TotalCharges values remained in the dataset.

• The tenure variable contained 604 missing observations. Since tenure is a numerical variable, the missing observations were imputed using the median value of 28 months calculated from the available tenure observations.

• Median imputation was selected because it provides a representative central value while being less influenced by unusually high or low tenure values than the mean. After imputation, the number of missing values in tenure reduced from 604 to 0, confirming successful completion of the treatment.

Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is performed to understand the characteristics of the customer base, identify important patterns in customer behaviour, and examine factors that may be associated with customer churn

UNIVARIATE ANALYSIS

Univariate analysis is used to understand the distribution of each individual variable, including customer characteristics, service usage, contract preferences and billing behaviour

In [76]:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# -----------------------------
# Define variables
# -----------------------------

categorical_cols = [
    'gender',
    'SeniorCitizen',
    'Partner',
    'Dependents',
    'PhoneService',
    'MultipleLines',
    'InternetService',
    'OnlineSecurity',
    'OnlineBackup',
    'DeviceProtection',
    'TechSupport',
    'StreamingTV',
    'StreamingMovies',
    'Contract',
    'PaperlessBilling',
    'PaymentMethod',
    'Churn'
]

numerical_cols = [
    'tenure',
    'MonthlyCharges',
    'TotalCharges'
]

# -----------------------------
# Categorical Variables
# -----------------------------

for col in categorical_cols:

    counts = df1[col].value_counts(dropna=False)
    percentages = counts / counts.sum() * 100

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))

    bars = plt.bar(
        counts.index.astype(str),
        counts.values
    )

    plt.title(f'Distribution of {col}', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    plt.xlabel(col)
    plt.ylabel('Number of Customers')
    plt.xticks(rotation=30, ha='right')

    # Percentage labels
    for bar, percentage in zip(bars, percentages):
        plt.text(
            bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2,
            bar.get_height(),
            f'{percentage:.1f}%',
            ha='center',
            va='bottom',
            fontsize=10
        )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


# -----------------------------
# Numerical Variables
# -----------------------------

for col in numerical_cols:

    mean_value = df1[col].mean()
    median_value = df1[col].median()

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))

    plt.hist(
        df1[col],
        bins=30,
        edgecolor='black'
    )

    plt.axvline(
        mean_value,
        linestyle='--',
        linewidth=2,
        label=f'Mean = {mean_value:.2f}'
    )

    plt.axvline(
        median_value,
        linestyle=':',
        linewidth=2,
        label=f'Median = {median_value:.2f}'
    )

    plt.title(f'Distribution of {col}', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    plt.xlabel(col)
    plt.ylabel('Number of Customers')
    plt.legend()

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

  1. Gender: Male customers account for 55.7%, while female customers account for 44.3%. The customer base therefore has a slightly higher proportion of male customers. However, the distribution is reasonably balanced between the two groups.

  2. SeniorCitizen: 88.2% of customers are non-senior citizens, while 11.8% are senior citizens. The customer base is therefore predominantly made up of non-senior customers.

  3. Partner: 58.0% of customers do not have a partner, while 42.0% have a partner. Customers without a partner form a moderately larger group.

  4. Dependents: 73.4% of customers do not have dependents, while 26.6% have dependents. The majority of customers therefore do not have dependents.

  5. PhoneService: 89.1% of customers have phone service, while 10.9% do not. Phone service is therefore used by the vast majority of customers.

  6. MultipleLines: 46.0% of customers have multiple lines. 43.2% have a single phone line/no multiple lines. 10.9% do not have phone service. The two main groups are relatively close in size.

  7. InternetService: 40.5% of customers use fibre optic internet. 36.1% use DSL. 23.4% do not have internet service. Fibre optic is the most common internet service, followed by DSL.

  8. OnlineSecurity: 52.4% of customers do not have online security. 24.1% have online security. 23.4% do not have internet service. More than half of the customers do not use online security services.

  9. OnlineBackup: 49.4% of customers do not have online backup. 27.1% have online backup. 23.4% do not have internet service. Customers without online backup form the largest group.

  10. DeviceProtection: 38.3% of customers have device protection. 38.3% do not have device protection. 23.4% do not have internet service. Among customers with internet service, device protection is almost evenly divided between users and non-users.

  11. TechSupport: 51.7% of customers do not have technical support. 24.8% have technical support. 23.4% do not have internet service. More than half of the customers do not subscribe to technical support.

  12. StreamingTV: 41.5% of customers do not use streaming TV. 35.0% use streaming TV. 23.4% do not have internet service. Streaming TV usage is relatively common, although non-users form the larger group.

  13. StreamingMovies: 42.0% of customers do not use streaming movies. 34.6% use streaming movies. 23.4% do not have internet service. Non-users slightly outnumber customers who use streaming movie services.

  14. Contract: 54.4% of customers are on month-to-month contracts. 24.4% have two-year contracts. 21.2% have one-year contracts. Month-to-month contracts are clearly the most common type.

  15. PaperlessBilling: 51.1% of customers use paperless billing. 48.9% do not use paperless billing. The distribution is almost evenly divided between the two groups.

  16. PaymentMethod: 34.4% use electronic checks. 24.3% use automatic credit card payments. 21.4% use mailed checks. 19.9% use automatic bank transfers. Electronic check is the most commonly used payment method.

  17. Churn: 71.8% of customers have not churned. 28.2% of customers have churned. The dataset therefore contains substantially more customers who stayed than customers who left.

  18. Tenure: The average customer tenure is 31.25 months, while the median is 28 months. Customers are spread across different tenure levels, with a noticeable concentration among newer customers. The difference between the mean and median indicates that some customers have considerably longer relationships with the company.

  19. MonthlyCharges: The average monthly charge is 64.88, while the median is 71.63. Monthly charges range from approximately 15.29 to 149.04. A sizeable group of customers has relatively low monthly charges, while many customers fall in the middle-to-higher charge range.

  20. TotalCharges: The average total charge is 2,228.86, while the median is 1,373.05. Total charges range from 0 to approximately 9,806.54. Many customers have relatively low total charges, while a smaller number of long-term customers have much higher accumulated charges.

Bivariate analysis¶

Bivariate analysis is performed to understand how individual customer characteristics and service-related factors are associated with customer churn. By comparing each variable with the churn outcome, we can identify customer groups that show relatively higher or lower levels of churn. This helps in understanding which customer characteristics and service factors may be important for customer retention.

For categorical varibale

In [77]:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

categorical_vars = [
    'gender',
    'SeniorCitizen',
    'Partner',
    'Dependents',
    'PhoneService',
    'MultipleLines',
    'InternetService',
    'OnlineSecurity',
    'OnlineBackup',
    'DeviceProtection',
    'TechSupport',
    'StreamingTV',
    'StreamingMovies',
    'Contract',
    'PaperlessBilling',
    'PaymentMethod'
]

for var in categorical_vars:

    percentage = pd.crosstab(
        df1[var],
        df1['Churn'],
        normalize='index'
    ) * 100

    ax = percentage.plot(
        kind='bar',
        stacked=True,
        figsize=(9, 5)
    )

    plt.title(f'{var} vs Churn', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
    plt.xlabel(var)
    plt.ylabel('Percentage of Customers')
    plt.xticks(rotation=35, ha='right')
    plt.ylim(0, 100)

    # Add percentage labels
    for container in ax.containers:
        labels = [
            f'{bar.get_height():.1f}%'
            if bar.get_height() > 3 else ''
            for bar in container
        ]

        ax.bar_label(
            container,
            labels=labels,
            label_type='center',
            fontsize=9
        )

    plt.legend(
        title='Churn',
        loc='upper right'
    )

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

  1. Contract vs Churn Customers on month-to-month contracts show the highest churn, with 46.0% of customers in this group having churned. Churn is much lower among customers on one-year contracts (11.3%) and two-year contracts (3.3%).This shows a clear association between contract duration and customer churn, with longer-term contracts being associated with lower observed churn.

  2. Tenure vs Churn Customers who churned generally have shorter tenure compared with customers who stayed. The median tenure of customers who stayed is approximately 35 months, while the median tenure of customers who churned is approximately 11 months. This indicates that customers in the earlier stages of their relationship with AlphaCom show higher observed churn.

  3. Internet Service vs Churn Customers using Fiber optic service have the highest observed churn, at 44.9%. Churn among DSL customers is 21.7%, while customers with no internet service have a lower churn rate of 9.4%. This suggests that internet service type is associated with differences in customer churn and should be considered when identifying potential churn drivers.

  4. Payment Method vs Churn Customers using electronic check have the highest observed churn, at 49.1%. Churn is considerably lower among customers using mailed check (22.2%), bank transfer (15.9%), and credit card (14.1%). The difference suggests that payment method is associated with customer churn and may provide a useful customer segment for further investigation.

  5. Online Security vs Churn Customers without online security have an observed churn rate of 43.0%, compared with 14.4% among customers with online security. Customers with no internet service have a lower churn rate of 9.4%. This indicates a noticeable difference in churn behaviour based on online security availability.

  6. Technical Support vs Churn Customers without technical support have a churn rate of 44.1%, compared with 12.9% among customers with technical support. Customers with no internet service have a churn rate of 9.4%. The difference indicates that technical support availability is associated with customer churn and may be an important factor to examine further.

  7. Senior Citizen Status vs Churn 42.5% of senior-citizen customers have churned, compared with 26.3% of non-senior customers. This shows a higher observed churn rate among senior-citizen customers. Senior-citizen status may therefore be useful as a customer characteristic when analysing churn patterns.

  8. Contract and Payment Method vs Churn The combination of contract type and payment method shows that churn varies substantially across customer segments. The highest observed churn is among month-to-month customers using electronic check (58.8%). Month-to-month customers using bank transfer, credit card and mailed check also show relatively high churn compared with customers on longer-term contracts. For one-year and two-year contracts, churn remains considerably lower across payment methods, indicating that contract duration remains an important factor when examining payment-related churn patterns.

For numerical variable

Since Churn has two categories (no and yes), we will use box plots to compare the distributions of these numerical variables between customers who stayed and those who churned.

In [78]:

•Tenure vs Churn Customers who churned generally have shorter tenure, with a median tenure of approximately 11 months, compared with 35 months for customers who stayed. This indicates that customers in the earlier stages of their relationship with AlphaCom show higher observed churn.

• Monthly Charges vs Churn Customers who churned tend to have higher monthly charges, with a median of approximately dollar79, compared with $66 among customers who stayed. This suggests that monthly cost may be an important factor associated with customer churn.

• Total Charges vs Churn Customers who churned generally have lower total charges, with a median of approximately dollar 1,000, compared with around dollar 1,330 for customers who stayed. This is consistent with the shorter tenure observed among churned customers, as customers who leave earlier have had less time to accumulate total charges.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Create a numeric version of Churn
df1['Churn_numeric'] = df1['Churn'].map({'no': 0, 'yes': 1})

# Select numerical variables
corr_cols = [
    'SeniorCitizen',
    'tenure',
    'MonthlyCharges',
    'TotalCharges',
    'Churn_numeric'
]

corr_matrix = df1[corr_cols].corr()

# Plot heatmap
plt.figure(figsize=(9, 6))

sns.heatmap(
    corr_matrix,
    annot=True,
    fmt='.2f',
    cmap='coolwarm',
    center=0,
    linewidths=0.5,
    square=True
)

plt.title('Correlation Heatmap of Numerical Variables', fontsize=16, fontweight='bold')
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')
plt.yticks(rotation=0)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

• The correlation analysis shows that tenure has the strongest relationship with churn among the numerical variables, with a correlation of -0.35, indicating that customers with longer tenure tend to show lower churn.

• Total charges have a weaker negative relationship with churn (-0.20), while monthly charges show a weak positive relationship (0.19). Senior citizen status has a relatively weak relationship with churn (0.12).

# Outlier Check using IQR method

numerical_cols = ['tenure', 'MonthlyCharges', 'TotalCharges']

for col in numerical_cols:

    Q1 = df1[col].quantile(0.25)
    Q3 = df1[col].quantile(0.75)
    IQR = Q3 - Q1

    lower_limit = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
    upper_limit = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR

    outliers = df1[
        (df1[col] < lower_limit) |
        (df1[col] > upper_limit)
    ]

    print(f'\n{col}')
    print(f'Lower limit: {lower_limit:.2f}')
    print(f'Upper limit: {upper_limit:.2f}')
    print(f'Number of outliers: {len(outliers)}')

•The boxplot shows that these are high TotalCharges values, but they are not necessarily errors. A customer who has stayed longer can naturally have a high total charge. So we should investigate these observations before deciding on treatment.

Outlier Analysis:

•Tenure: The boxplot shows no statistical outliers, indicating that the tenure values fall within the expected range. Therefore, no outlier treatment was required for this variable. The negative tenure values identified earlier were treated separately as anomalous values because negative tenure is not logically valid.

•MonthlyCharges: No statistical outliers were identified in the boxplot. The charges are distributed within the expected range, so no outlier treatment was required.

•TotalCharges: The IQR-based analysis identified 75 high-value observations above 8,233.95, ranging from 8,238.59 to 10,325.98. These customers had relatively long tenures, with an average tenure of approximately 66 months, which explains their higher cumulative charges. Hence, these observations were considered valid customer records and were retained for further analysis.

**No additional feature engineering was required, as the existing variables adequately captured the customer, service, contract, and billing characteristics needed for churn analysis and modelling.

Model Prediction

Model can make wrong predictions as: Predicting a customer will not churn when, in reality, the customer will churn. This is a False Negative (FN). Predicting a customer will churn when, in reality, the customer will not churn. This is a False Positive (FP).

Which case is more important?

For the customer churn problem, False Negatives are particularly important because when an actual churner is predicted as a non-churner, the business may miss the opportunity to take preventive retention actions.

False Positives are also important because the company may spend retention resources on customers who were not actually going to churn.

Therefore, the model should identify as many actual churn customers as possible while also maintaining a reasonable level of precision.

Since the objective is to identify customers who are likely to churn, missing an actual churn customer (False Negative) may result in a missed opportunity for the company to take timely retention action. Therefore, Recall is selected as the primary metric, as it focuses on correctly identifying actual churn customers.

Recall measures the proportion of actual churn customers correctly identified by the model. A higher recall means fewer actual churn customers are missed by the model.

Precision, F1-score and Accuracy are also considered to provide a comprehensive assessment of model performance rather than relying on Recall alone.

ROC-AUC is used to evaluate the model's ability to distinguish between churn and non-churn customers across different classification thresholds.

# Import libraries required for model evaluation
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    recall_score,
    precision_score,
    f1_score,

In [97]:
# Define a function to calculate classification performance metrics
def model_performance_classification_statsmodels(
    model, predictors, target, threshold=0.5
):
    """
    Calculate performance metrics for a classification model.

    model: fitted classification model
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    threshold: probability threshold for class 1
    """

    # Convert predicted probabilities into class predictions
    pred_temp = model.predict(predictors) >=threshold
    pred = np.round(pred_temp)

    # Calculate evaluation metrics
    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)

    # Store metrics in a DataFrame
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Accuracy": acc,
            "Recall": recall,
            "Precision": precision,
            "F1": f1,
        },
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf
In [98]:
# Define a function to plot the confusion matrix
def confusion_matrix_statsmodels(
    model, predictors, target, threshold=0.5
):
    """
    Plot the confusion matrix with counts and percentages.
    """

    # Generate class predictions using the specified threshold
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors) > threshold

    # Create confusion matrix
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)

    # Create labels showing count and percentage
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    # Plot confusion matrix
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")
    plt.title("Confusion Matrix - Baseline Logistic Regression")
    plt.show()

• The baseline Logistic Regression model achieved an Accuracy of 75.28%, Recall of 79.84%, Precision of 52.81%, F1-score of 63.57%, and ROC-AUC of 84.87% on the test dataset.

• The confusion matrix shows that the model correctly identified 780 actual churn customers and 1,942 non-churn customers, while 197 actual churn customers were incorrectly classified as non-churn.

• Recall of 79.84% indicates that the model identified approximately 80% of actual churn customers.

• lower Precision of 52.81% indicates that a considerable proportion of customers predicted as churners were actually non-churners. These results establish the baseline performance for the churn prediction task.

Recall is ~79.8% on the test set, meaning the model identifies a relatively high proportion of actual churn customers. Since our business objective is to identify customers who are likely to churn, recall is an important metric. Test accuracy is 75.28%, while test F1-score is 63.57%.

The training and test results are reasonably close, so there is no obvious severe overfitting at this baseline stage.

Precision is lower (52.81%), meaning some customers predicted as churners do not actually churn. This is something we can try to improve later.

ROC-AUC: 0.8492

• The ROC curve evaluates the ability of the final Logistic Regression model to distinguish between customers who churn and those who do not churn across different classification thresholds.

• The model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.849, indicating good discriminatory ability. The curve remains substantially above the diagonal reference line, showing that the model performs considerably better than random classification. This suggests that the model is effective at ranking customers according to their likelihood of churn.

In [119]:
# Precision-Recall Curve for the Final Logistic Regression Model

from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Calculate precision and recall values
precision, recall, pr_thresholds = precision_recall_curve(
    y_test,
    test_prob
)

# Calculate Average Precision
average_precision = average_precision_score(y_test, test_prob)

# Plot Precision-Recall curve
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))

plt.plot(
    recall,
    precision,
    label=f'Logistic Regression (AP = {average_precision:.3f})'
)

plt.xlabel('Recall')
plt.ylabel('Precision')
plt.title('Precision-Recall Curve - Final Logistic Regression')
plt.legend()
plt.grid()

plt.show()

print("Average Precision:", round(average_precision, 4))

Average Precision: 0.6679

• The Precision–Recall curve illustrates the trade-off between precision and recall at different classification thresholds. The final Logistic Regression model achieved an Average Precision (AP) of 0.668.

• The curve shows that precision decreases as recall increases, which is expected because identifying more potential churners generally results in more false-positive predictions.

• The curve therefore helps assess the model's performance particularly in identifying the churn class, which is important given the class imbalance in the dataset.

In [120]:
# Find the optimal threshold using the Precision-Recall curve
# using the F1-score as the selection criterion

f1_scores = (
    2 * precision[:-1] * recall[:-1]
    / (precision[:-1] + recall[:-1] + 1e-10)
)

optimal_index = np.argmax(f1_scores)

optimal_threshold = pr_thresholds[optimal_index]
optimal_precision = precision[optimal_index]
optimal_recall = recall[optimal_index]
optimal_f1 = f1_scores[optimal_index]

print("Optimal threshold:", round(optimal_threshold, 4))
print("Precision at optimal threshold:", round(optimal_precision, 4))
print("Recall at optimal threshold:", round(optimal_recall, 4))
print("F1-score at optimal threshold:", round(optimal_f1, 4))

Optimal threshold: 0.6097
Precision at optimal threshold: 0.5847
Recall at optimal threshold: 0.7175
F1-score at optimal threshold: 0.6443

• The default classification threshold of 0.50 was further evaluated using the Precision–Recall curve to identify a threshold that provides a better balance between precision and recall.

• The analysis identified an optimal threshold of 0.6097, at which the model achieved Precision = 0.5847, Recall = 0.7175, and F1-score = 0.6443. Compared with the default threshold, this threshold provides a more balanced classification of churn customers by maintaining relatively high recall while improving the precision–recall trade-off. Therefore, 0.6097 was selected as the operating threshold for the final Logistic Regression model.

Advanced Model Building¶

Decision Tree Classifier

The Decision Tree is used to predict whether a customer is likely to churn or remain with AlphaCom. It helps identify the customer characteristics and conditions that are associated with churn and provides an easy-to-understand model for analysing customer behaviour. The model also provides a useful baseline for comparing the performance of more advanced ensemble models used later in the analysis.

In [121]:
# Import libraries required for calculating model performance
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    recall_score,
    precision_score,
    f1_score,
    roc_auc_score
)

# Import pandas for creating the performance table
import pandas as pd


# Define a function to calculate classification performance
def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):

    # Generate predictions
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    # Generate probability predictions for the churn class
    pred_prob = model.predict_proba(predictors)[:, 1]

    # Calculate performance metrics
    accuracy = accuracy_score(target, pred)
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)
    roc_auc = roc_auc_score(target, pred_prob)

    # Store the results in a DataFrame
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame({
        "Accuracy": [accuracy],
        "Recall": [recall],
        "Precision": [precision],
        "F1-Score": [f1],
        "ROC-AUC": [roc_auc]
    })

    # Return the performance results
    return df_perf
In [122]:
# Import libraries required for the confusion matrix
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix


# Define a function to display the confusion matrix
def confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, predictors, target):

    # Generate predictions
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    # Calculate the confusion matrix
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, pred)

    # Calculate the percentage represented by each cell
    cm_percent = cm / cm.sum() * 100

    # Create an empty array for the cell labels
    annot_labels = np.empty_like(cm).astype(object)

    # Add count and percentage to each cell
    for i in range(cm.shape[0]):
        for j in range(cm.shape[1]):
            annot_labels[i, j] = (
                f"{cm[i, j]}\n"
                f"{cm_percent[i, j]:.2f}%"
            )

    # Create the confusion matrix plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6))

    # Plot the confusion matrix
    sns.heatmap(
        cm,
        annot=annot_labels,
        fmt="",
        cmap="magma",
        cbar=True,
        linewidths=0.5,
        xticklabels=["0", "1"],
        yticklabels=["0", "1"]
    )

    # Add axis labels
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")
    plt.ylabel("True label")

    # Add title
    plt.title("Confusion Matrix")

    # Display the plot
    plt.show()

Model Performance Comparison

• The six advanced classification models were evaluated on the test dataset using Accuracy, Recall, Precision, F1-Score, and ROC-AUC. Since the primary business objective is to identify customers who are likely to churn, Recall is considered the primary metric, while the other metrics are used to provide a broader assessment of model performance.

• The Decision Tree records the lowest overall performance, with 55.68% recall and 66.35% ROC-AUC. Bagging, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost provide comparatively stronger overall performance across the evaluation metrics.

• AdaBoost achieves the highest recall of 79.22%, meaning it identifies the largest proportion of actual churn customers among the six models.

• Gradient Boosting achieves the highest ROC-AUC of 85.15% and an F1-score of 63.74%, while also maintaining a recall of 72.16%.

• Random Forest and XGBoost both achieve 78.10% accuracy, although their recall values are lower than those of AdaBoost and Gradient Boosting.

Overall, the results show differences in how the models balance the identification of churners with the avoidance of incorrect predictions. Therefore, the models with comparatively stronger performance will be considered for further hyperparameter tuning to determine whether their performance can be improved.

Model Performance Improvement Using Hyperparameter Tuning¶

• Based on the initial model evaluation, AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, and Random Forest were selected for hyperparameter tuning. The train–test performance comparison indicated substantial generalisation gaps for Decision Tree, Bagging, and Random Forest, while AdaBoost and Gradient Boosting showed comparatively smaller gaps.

• AdaBoost achieved a strong test Recall (0.7922) and F1-Score (0.6336), which are relevant for identifying customers at risk of churn. Gradient Boosting achieved the highest test F1-Score (0.6374) and a strong ROC-AUC (0.8515), indicating good discriminatory performance.

• Random Forest achieved a test ROC-AUC of 0.8291 and F1-Score of 0.6118, while its high training performance suggested potential for improvement through complexity control and hyperparameter optimisation. Therefore, Random Forest, AdaBoost, and Gradient Boosting were selected for hyperparameter tuning to investigate whether their generalisation performance could be improved on unseen data.

Hyperparameter Tuning – Random Forest

In [154]:
# Import the Random Forest classifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

# Import GridSearchCV for hyperparameter tuning
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

# Choose the type of classifier
rf_estimator = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=1)

# Grid of parameters to choose from
parameters = {
    "n_estimators": [75, 100, 125],
    "max_features": [0.8, 0.9, 1.0],
    "max_samples": [0.8, 0.9, 1.0]
}

# Run the grid search using Recall as the scoring metric
grid_obj = GridSearchCV(
    rf_estimator,
    parameters,
    scoring="recall",
    cv=5,
    n_jobs=-1
)

# Fit Grid Search on the SMOTE-balanced training data
grid_obj = grid_obj.fit(
    X_train_smote,
    y_train_smote
)

# Set the classifier to the best combination of parameters
rf_estimator = grid_obj.best_estimator_

# Fit the best algorithm to the SMOTE-balanced training data
rf_estimator.fit(
    X_train_smote,
    y_train_smote
)

• The test-set performance of the classification models is compared using Accuracy, Recall, Precision, F1-Score and ROC-AUC. The results show that the models have different strengths across the evaluation metrics.

• Among the tuned models, Tuned Random Forest achieves an Accuracy of 78.07%, while Tuned AdaBoost achieves the highest Recall of 97.75%. Tuned Gradient Boosting achieves a Recall of 85.36% and the highest ROC-AUC of 83.36% among the tuned models.

• The three tuned models — Random Forest, AdaBoost and Gradient Boosting — were evaluated on the test set using Accuracy, Recall, Precision, F1-Score and ROC-AUC. Since the primary business objective is to identify customers who are at high risk of churn, Recall was considered the primary metric of choice.

• Tuned AdaBoost achieved the highest Recall of 0.9775, identifying approximately 97.75% of actual churners in the test set. Tuned Gradient Boosting achieved a Recall of 0.8536, while Tuned Random Forest achieved 0.6592.

• Although Random Forest achieved higher Precision and F1-Score, and Gradient Boosting achieved the highest ROC-AUC, both models had lower Recall than AdaBoost.

• Therefore, considering the primary objective of minimising missed churners, Tuned AdaBoost was selected as the final model. Its lower Precision and F1-Score indicate a trade-off, as the model identifies more potential churners at the cost of generating more false-positive churn predictions.

• The tuned AdaBoost model correctly identified 955 out of 977 actual churners, resulting in a high recall of 97.75% and only 22 false negatives. However, the model generated 1,784 false positives, indicating that a substantial number of non-churning customers were incorrectly classified as potential churners. This explains the relatively low precision of 34.87%.

• Given the business objective of proactively identifying customers at risk of churn, the high recall indicates that the model is effective at capturing potential churners, although the associated false-positive rate should be considered when designing retention campaigns.

• The tuned AdaBoost model achieved a recall of 97.75% for the Churn class, indicating that it identifies the vast majority of customers who actually churn. This is important in the context of AlphaCom's objective of proactively identifying customers at risk of churn. However, the model's precision for the Churn class is 34.87%, indicating that a substantial proportion of customers identified as potential churners do not actually churn. The model therefore prioritises capturing potential churners, resulting in a higher number of false-positive predictions. The ROC-AUC of 78.20% indicates a reasonable ability to distinguish between churn and non-churn customers.

• Based on the business objective of identifying as many potential churners as possible, with Recall as the primary evaluation metric, Tuned AdaBoost was selected as the final model. Its test-set recall of 97.75% indicates that it captures most of the actual churners, although this comes with a trade-off in precision and overall accuracy.

Key Insights

  • Customers’ contract type plays an important role in their likelihood of leaving AlphaCom, making contract-related customers an important group for retention efforts.
  • Electronic check users are an important customer group to monitor, as their payment method is strongly associated with identifying customers who may leave.
  • Customer tenure matters — customers at different stages of their relationship with AlphaCom may have different retention needs.
  • AlphaCom has an opportunity to identify customers who may leave before they actually leave, allowing the company to take preventive action.

Recommendations

  • Offer personalised renewal plans and suitable incentives to customers who may be at risk of leaving.
  • Review the payment experience of electronic check users and make billing and payment processes easier and more convenient.
  • Provide strong onboarding and early support to newer customers to build a lasting relationship with AlphaCom.
  • Contact customers showing signs of leaving before they cancel their service, understand their concerns and provide appropriate solutions.
  • Use targeted retention offers instead of giving the same offer to every customer.
  • Regularly collect customer feedback and address billing, service and support concerns to prevent avoidable customer losses.
  • By taking action before customers leave, AlphaCom can reduce churn, protect revenue and improve customer lifetime value, which directly supports the project's objective.
